newsitem.title: USA: U.S. airline start-ups blocked by majors - GAO study.
newsitem.headline: U.S. airline start-ups blocked by majors - GAO study.

text.p: Despite airline deregulation nearly 20 years ago, major U.S. airlines have blocked start-up carriers from entering some markets, the General Accounting Office of the U.S. Congress reported on Wednesday.
This, the GAO report said, leads to higher fares.
It said access to airports continues to be impeded by federal limits on takeoffs and landings at Kennedy and LaGuardia airports in New York, Washington National airport and Chicago O'Hare airport.

The GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, also said that new airlines were stymied by the long-term exclusive gate leases the majors have and rules at LaGuardia and Washington that prohibit flights that exceed certain distances.
While these barriers can affect any airline, they mainly hit the newer ones because the older carriers hold nearly all of the slots and the gate leases, it said.

"These barriers particularly impede the entry of newer airlines into key markets in the East and upper Midwest because several airports in those regions have leased most of thier gates to one airline," the report said.

Even where airport access is not a problem, it said, established airlines often try to keep out others by paying bonuses to travel agents, by beneficial frequent-flyer plans and by code sharing partnerships with commuter airlines.
As a result of these marketing strategies, the report said, "competition suffers, leading to higher air fares."
It added that the effect of these strategies was greatest -- and fares the highest -- in markets where the dominant carrier's position is protected by operating barriers.
But it said the effect on quality of service is difficult to measure, because where the barriers reduce competition, consumers often get benefits in other ways, such as free frequent flyer trips.
